promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Speed, velocity, acceleration and motion graphs

questions.q: Which quantity is a vector because it has both magnitude and direction?
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector as it specifies both how fast an object moves and its direction, whereas speed is a scalar.

questions.q: Which equation correctly gives average speed?
questions.explain: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken.

questions.q: What does the gradient (slope) of a distance-time graph represent?
questions.explain: On a distance-time graph the gradient equals change in distance over change in time, which is the speed.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explain: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is change in velocity over time, which is the acceleration.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explain: Multiplying velocity by time gives distance, so the area beneath a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled.

questions.q: A distance-time graph shows a horizontal (flat) line. What is the object doing?
questions.explain: A flat line means distance is not changing over time, so the object is at rest.

questions.q: Which equation defines acceleration?
options: acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken
questions.explain: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, calculated as the change in velocity divided by the time taken.

questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = (20 − 0) ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².

questions.q: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s.

questions.q: Newton's first law states that an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by what?
questions.explain: Newton's first law: motion only changes when a non-zero resultant force acts on the object.

questions.q: Which equation states Newton's second law?
questions.explain: Newton's second law relates resultant force to mass and acceleration as F = ma.

questions.q: Newton's third law states that when object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts a force on A that is:
options: Larger and in the same direction
Equal in size and opposite in direction
Equal in size and in the same direction
questions.explain: Newton's third law: forces occur in pairs that are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, acting on different objects.

questions.q: What happens to the acceleration of an object if the resultant force on it doubles while its mass stays the same?
questions.explain: Since a = F ÷ m, acceleration is directly proportional to force, so doubling the force doubles the acceleration.

questions.q: A car travels at a steady velocity along a straight road. What is true about the forces on it?
options: The driving force is greater than the resistive forces
questions.explain: Constant velocity means balanced forces, so the resultant force is zero (Newton's first law).

questions.q: A resultant force of 2000 N acts on a car of mass 1000 kg. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Using a = F ÷ m = 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 m/s².

questions.q: A trolley of mass 1500 kg moves at 20 m/s. What is its momentum? (p = mv)
questions.explain: Momentum = mass × velocity = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s.

questions.q: The stopping distance of a vehicle is made up of which two parts?
questions.explain: Stopping distance = thinking distance (during the driver's reaction time) + braking distance (while braking).

questions.q: Which of these increases the driver's THINKING distance?
options: Being tired or under the influence of alcohol
questions.explain: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions lengthen reaction time, increasing the thinking distance.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the BRAKING distance of a car?
options: A wet or icy road surface
questions.explain: Reduced friction between tyres and a wet or icy road means a greater distance is needed to stop while braking.

questions.q: If a car's speed increases, how does its stopping distance change?
questions.explain: Both thinking and braking distances grow with speed, so a higher speed gives a longer overall stopping distance.
